fields.ch00-02: Research on how we trust, question, and make sense of AI — especially when the answers matter.
fields.ch00-05: I'm Minseo, a researcher interested in the moments when human judgment meets intelligent systems. This is a little book about my work, the ideas behind it, and what I hope to understand next.
fields.ch01-01:
A little about
the person
behind the questions.
fields.ch01-02: I'm an interdisciplinary researcher exploring how people think, feel, and make decisions in AI-mediated environments.
fields.ch01-03: My work sits at the intersection of Human–AI Interaction, health communication, and behavioral research. I am especially interested in what happens when AI tools communicate uncertain health information, and how their design shapes human understanding.
fields.ch01-04: Before working on health-related AI experiences, I studied data science and built interactive systems. That path made me curious about a question that code alone cannot answer: how do people actually experience the technologies we create?
fields.ch01-05: I want to design intelligent systems that help people think more clearly, not simply feel more certain.

fields.ch02-01:

an answer,
what do we hear?
fields.ch02-02: AI can make advice feel immediate, accessible, and personal. But its wording can also shape what we notice, fear, or believe.
fields.ch02-03: How do communication cues change our trust and judgment?
fields.ch02-04: I study how the source of advice (AI or human) and small identification cues influence how personally attentive a consultation feels — and how people assess uncertain health information.

fields.ch05-02: An informal notebook for the ideas that don't quite fit into an abstract.
fields.ch05-04: In health conversations, words can be more than information. A confident tone can calm us down, but it can also make an uncertain claim feel settled.
fields.ch05-05: That tension makes communication design a research problem. When does a system help someone navigate uncertainty? When does it accidentally encourage them to stop asking questions?
fields.ch05-06: I want to understand that boundary — and design for the space around it.
fields.ch05-08: Every study begins with an assumption. These are the ones I keep examining.
fields.ch05-09: Small details — such as acknowledging someone's context — may change how attentively a response is perceived, even when its core information stays the same.
fields.ch05-10: The same words can carry different expectations when attributed to a human clinician or to an AI assistant. Source cues may shape trust and accountability.
fields.ch05-11: An early suggestion can remain an anchor as more information arrives. How could systems help people revise first impressions rather than merely reinforce them?
